CourseName: CEN3722 - Introduction to Human Computer Interfaces

Outcomes.Text: Explain how AI coding assistants such as Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, and Codex integrate into HCI design and development pipelines.
Identify the strengths and limitations of AI-assisted tools when applied to prototyping and interface design tasks.
Apply AI coding assistants to accelerate prototyping workflows while preserving design quality and usability standards.
Demonstrate practical techniques for prompting AI tools to generate, refine, and iterate on design and code artifacts.
Analyze the impact of AI-assisted workflows on collaboration, iteration speed, and design decision-making in HCI projects.
Evaluate outputs from AI coding assistants for design accuracy, accessibility, and alignment with user-centered design principles.

Topics.Title: Introduction to AI Coding Assistants in HCI
Topics.Summary: Provides an overview of leading AI coding assistants and establishes how they fit within modern HCI design and development contexts. Sets the foundation for understanding tool capabilities and appropriate use cases.

Elements.Title: What Are AI Coding Assistants?
Elements.BodyText: AI coding assistants are software tools powered by large language models that can generate, complete, explain, and refactor code in response to natural language prompts or partial code input.
Elements.Notes: Examples include GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, and Anthropic's Claude Code. Each tool has different strengths: Copilot excels at in-editor autocomplete, Codex at programmatic API-driven generation, and Claude Code at reasoning through complex multi-step development tasks.

Items.Text: AI coding assistants use large language models trained on large corpora of code and documentation.
They accept natural language descriptions, existing code, or a combination of both as input.
Outputs can include full functions, boilerplate components, test cases, and explanatory comments.
These tools are integrated into IDEs, terminals, and browser-based environments.

Elements.Title: Key Tools: Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, and Codex
Elements.BodyText: Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, and OpenAI Codex represent three distinct but complementary approaches to AI-assisted development, each offering unique integration points and interaction models.
Elements.Notes: GitHub Copilot is deeply embedded in VS Code and JetBrains IDEs, making it the most common entry point for developers. Codex underpins many third-party tools and is accessible via API. Claude Code is notable for its ability to handle longer context and multi-file reasoning tasks, which is valuable for complex HCI projects.

Items.Text: GitHub Copilot integrates directly into popular IDEs and provides real-time inline code suggestions.
OpenAI Codex is accessible via API and powers a wide range of custom developer tooling.
Claude Code is designed for agentic, multi-step tasks that require sustained reasoning across larger codebases.
Each tool differs in context window size, integration method, and handling of design-related code.

Elements.Title: The Role of AI in the HCI Pipeline
Elements.BodyText: Within the HCI pipeline, AI assistants can contribute at multiple stages including requirements gathering, wireframing support, component generation, and usability testing scaffolding.
Elements.Notes: HCI pipelines traditionally include research, ideation, prototyping, evaluation, and iteration. AI tools primarily accelerate the prototyping and iteration phases but can also assist in generating user personas, synthesizing research notes, and drafting accessibility documentation.

Items.Text: AI assistants are most impactful during the prototyping and iterative refinement stages of HCI projects.
They can generate UI component scaffolding, reducing the time from wireframe to interactive prototype.
AI tools can assist with generating accessibility markup and ARIA annotations in interface code.
Human judgment remains essential for interpreting user research and making design decisions.

Elements.Title: Opportunities and Limitations of AI-Assisted Design
Elements.BodyText: While AI coding assistants can significantly accelerate development velocity, they also introduce risks such as generating technically correct but design-inappropriate code, reinforcing common patterns over novel solutions, and producing inaccessible interfaces.
Elements.Notes: A common pitfall is accepting AI-generated UI components that follow generic web patterns rather than the specific design system of the project. Students should be encouraged to treat AI output as a first draft requiring critical review, not a finished deliverable.

Items.Text: AI assistants can reduce repetitive coding tasks, freeing designers and developers to focus on higher-order decisions.
Generated code may not align with project-specific design systems, brand guidelines, or accessibility requirements.
AI tools can introduce subtle biases from their training data, favoring dominant design patterns.
Over-reliance on AI suggestions can limit the development of foundational design and coding skills.

Topics.Title: Effective Prompting Strategies for Design Tasks
Topics.Summary: Teaches students how to construct clear, context-rich prompts that guide AI assistants toward producing useful design and development outputs. Covers prompt structure, iterative refinement, and domain-specific prompting conventions.

Elements.Title: Principles of Effective Prompting
Elements.BodyText: Effective prompting involves providing the AI with sufficient context about the task, the target user, the technology stack, and the desired output format to generate relevant and actionable results.
Elements.Notes: A useful mental model is to treat the AI as a skilled but context-free contractor: the more precise your brief, the better the output. Vague prompts such as 'make a login form' yield generic results, while prompts specifying framework, accessibility requirements, and visual constraints yield far more usable outputs.

Items.Text: Prompts should specify the technology stack, component type, and any design system constraints.
Including the intended user context or task scenario helps the AI generate more appropriate interface code.
Requesting a specific output format, such as a React component or an HTML/CSS snippet, reduces ambiguity.
Breaking complex design tasks into smaller, sequential prompts improves output quality and traceability.

Elements.Title: Iterative Prompt Refinement
Elements.BodyText: AI-assisted design is rarely a single-step process; effective practitioners treat initial outputs as drafts and use follow-up prompts to refine, constrain, or redirect the AI toward better solutions.
Elements.Notes: Iterative prompting mirrors design iteration itself. Students can apply familiar HCI critique frameworks when reviewing AI output: Does this meet the user's needs? Does it follow established conventions? Is it accessible? The answers drive the next prompt.

Items.Text: Review AI-generated outputs critically before accepting them and identify specific gaps or errors.
Follow-up prompts can request adjustments to layout, color contrast, semantic HTML structure, or responsiveness.
Providing examples of desired output within the prompt, known as few-shot prompting, improves alignment.
Documenting the prompting sequence supports reproducibility and team collaboration.

Elements.Title: Prompting for Accessibility and Usability
Elements.BodyText: AI assistants require explicit instruction to generate code that meets accessibility standards such as WCAG 2.1, as they default to common patterns that may not be fully accessible.
Elements.Notes: Students should practice prompting specifically for ARIA roles, keyboard navigability, sufficient color contrast, and screen reader compatibility. Testing AI-generated components with accessibility checkers such as axe or Lighthouse is a recommended follow-up step.

Items.Text: Always specify accessibility requirements in the prompt, including WCAG level and relevant interaction patterns.
Request ARIA labels, roles, and live region attributes explicitly when generating interactive components.
Ask the AI to explain its accessibility choices so that omissions or errors become visible.
Validate AI-generated accessible code with automated tools before integrating it into a prototype.

Elements.Title: Design System Integration Through Prompting
Elements.BodyText: AI assistants can be guided to produce outputs consistent with an existing design system by providing component token names, style guide excerpts, or example components as part of the prompt context.
Elements.Notes: Some tools, such as GitHub Copilot, can learn project-specific conventions through extended use within a codebase. For one-off tasks, pasting relevant design token definitions or a component example into the prompt context is effective.

Items.Text: Include design token names, color variables, or typography scales in prompts to align outputs with the design system.
Providing a reference component as an example teaches the AI the expected code style and structure.
Request that the AI use only named design system components rather than inline styles or custom CSS.
Review outputs against the design system documentation to catch deviations before they propagate.

Elements.Title: Avoiding Common Prompting Pitfalls
Elements.BodyText: Several common mistakes reduce the quality of AI-assisted design outputs, including underspecifying context, accepting first outputs without review, and treating AI-generated code as production-ready.
Elements.Notes: A frequent error is asking the AI to 'fix' a problem without explaining what the desired behavior should be, leading to changes that solve the stated symptom while introducing new issues. Students should practice specifying both the current behavior and the intended behavior in correction prompts.

Items.Text: Underspecified prompts produce generic outputs that require significant rework to fit the project.
Accepting AI outputs without code review can introduce security vulnerabilities or accessibility failures.
Asking the AI to fix an issue without describing the intended outcome often shifts rather than resolves the problem.
Prompts should be versioned or logged so that successful patterns can be reused across the project.

Topics.Title: AI-Accelerated Prototyping Workflows
Topics.Summary: Covers practical workflows for integrating AI coding assistants into the prototyping phase of HCI projects, from low-fidelity scaffold generation to interactive prototype iteration. Emphasizes speed and quality trade-offs.

Elements.Title: From Wireframe to Code with AI
Elements.BodyText: AI coding assistants can dramatically reduce the time required to translate wireframes into interactive HTML, CSS, and JavaScript prototypes by generating layout scaffolding from natural language descriptions of the wireframe.
Elements.Notes: Some emerging tools can accept image inputs of wireframes and generate corresponding code directly. Even without image input, a detailed textual description of a wireframe layout can yield a usable prototype scaffold in minutes. The key skill is translating visual design intent into precise textual descriptions.

Items.Text: Describe the wireframe layout in terms of component hierarchy, spatial relationships, and interactive behaviors.
AI-generated scaffolds provide a starting structure that designers can refine rather than building from scratch.
Separating layout generation from styling prompts allows for cleaner, more maintainable output.
Validate the generated prototype against the original wireframe before investing time in further refinement.

Elements.Title: Rapid Component Generation
Elements.BodyText: One of the highest-value applications of AI in prototyping is the rapid generation of reusable UI components such as navigation bars, modal dialogs, forms, and data tables.
Elements.Notes: Students should develop a personal library of effective prompts for common HCI components. Reusing and refining these prompts across projects builds efficiency over time. Component generation works best when the target framework, such as React, Vue, or plain HTML, is specified upfront.

Items.Text: AI can generate framework-specific components including React, Vue, Svelte, or Web Components on demand.
Generated components should be reviewed for prop structure, event handling, and state management correctness.
Requesting unit test stubs alongside component generation supports quality assurance from the start.
Saving and annotating effective component prompts creates a reusable prompt library for future projects.

Elements.Title: Iterating on Prototypes with AI Assistance
Elements.BodyText: After an initial prototype is generated, AI assistants can support rapid iteration by modifying specific components, adjusting layouts, and incorporating feedback from usability evaluations.
Elements.Notes: When incorporating usability test feedback into prompts, it helps to describe the observed user behavior and the design goal rather than prescribing a specific solution. This allows the AI to suggest multiple approaches, which the designer can then evaluate.

Items.Text: Frame iteration prompts around observed usability issues and desired interaction outcomes.
AI can generate multiple design variations for the same component, supporting design comparison and A/B testing.
Use AI to quickly implement accessibility improvements identified during usability evaluations.
Track prompt-driven changes in version control to maintain a clear record of design evolution.

Elements.Title: Balancing Speed and Design Quality
Elements.BodyText: The speed advantage of AI-assisted prototyping must be balanced against the risk of accumulating design debt, where rapid generation produces code that is difficult to maintain, extend, or align with the broader design vision.
Elements.Notes: Design debt in AI-assisted projects often manifests as inconsistent component styles, redundant CSS, or inaccessible markup that was never reviewed. Establishing a lightweight review checklist for AI-generated outputs at each prototyping stage helps teams maintain quality without losing velocity.

Items.Text: Establish a review checklist for AI-generated prototype components covering accessibility, design system alignment, and code clarity.
Prioritize quality reviews at prototype milestones rather than reviewing every incremental AI-generated change.
Refactor AI-generated code periodically to remove redundancies and align with evolving design system conventions.
Communicate to stakeholders that AI-generated prototypes are exploratory artifacts, not production-ready deliverables.

Elements.Title: Integrating AI Tools into Team Workflows
Elements.BodyText: When working in teams, AI coding assistants must be integrated thoughtfully to ensure consistency, shared understanding, and equitable contribution across team members.
Elements.Notes: Teams should agree on which AI tools are approved for use, how AI-generated code should be documented and attributed, and how to handle disagreements about AI suggestions. Establishing a shared prompt library encourages consistency and helps onboard team members to effective AI use patterns.

Items.Text: Define team conventions for documenting AI-assisted contributions in commit messages and design notes.
Maintain a shared prompt library so that all team members benefit from collectively refined prompting strategies.
Assign human reviewers for all AI-generated outputs before they are merged into shared project branches.
Rotate AI-assisted tasks to ensure all team members develop proficiency with the tools.

Topics.Title: Maintaining Design Quality in AI-Assisted Projects
Topics.Summary: Addresses strategies and evaluation practices that ensure AI-generated outputs meet human-centered design standards. Covers review processes, quality criteria, and the designer's role in critically evaluating AI contributions.

Elements.Title: Defining Design Quality in the AI Context
Elements.BodyText: Design quality in AI-assisted projects encompasses not only visual fidelity but also usability, accessibility, performance, and alignment with user needs as surfaced through the HCI research process.
Elements.Notes: It is worth emphasizing that AI tools optimize for code correctness and pattern frequency, not for user experience quality. A component can be syntactically perfect and still fail a usability heuristic. Students should internalize that quality judgment remains a fundamentally human responsibility.

Items.Text: Design quality criteria include usability, accessibility, visual consistency, performance, and user need alignment.
AI tools do not inherently optimize for user experience; they optimize for pattern-matching to training data.
Quality standards should be documented in a project design brief before AI-assisted generation begins.
Regularly revisiting quality criteria throughout the project prevents gradual drift from the original design intent.

Elements.Title: Heuristic Evaluation of AI-Generated Interfaces
Elements.BodyText: Nielsen's ten usability heuristics provide a structured framework for evaluating AI-generated interface components and identifying usability issues that automated tools may miss.
Elements.Notes: Students should practice applying heuristics such as visibility of system status, user control and freedom, and error prevention specifically to AI-generated prototype components. This bridges familiar HCI theory with the practical realities of AI-assisted development.

Items.Text: Apply heuristic evaluation systematically to AI-generated prototypes at each major iteration checkpoint.
Focus especially on error handling, feedback mechanisms, and consistency heuristics, which AI often underserves.
Document heuristic violations as specific, actionable prompts for the next AI-assisted revision cycle.
Involve multiple evaluators to counteract individual blind spots when reviewing AI-generated interfaces.

Elements.Title: Accessibility Auditing of AI-Generated Code
Elements.BodyText: AI-generated interface code frequently requires accessibility remediation, making systematic auditing with both automated tools and manual testing an essential quality assurance step.
Elements.Notes: Automated tools such as axe DevTools, Lighthouse, and WAVE catch a significant proportion of WCAG violations but cannot replace manual keyboard navigation testing and screen reader evaluation. Students should develop a minimum viable accessibility audit practice for every AI-generated prototype.

Items.Text: Run automated accessibility checkers such as axe or Lighthouse on every AI-generated prototype before user testing.
Manually test keyboard navigation, focus management, and screen reader announcements in interactive components.
Document accessibility issues with reference to specific WCAG success criteria to guide targeted AI revision prompts.
Treat accessibility remediation as a non-negotiable quality gate, not an optional polish step.

Elements.Title: Code Review Practices for AI-Generated Output
Elements.BodyText: AI-generated code should be subject to the same code review practices as human-authored code, with additional attention to areas where AI tools commonly introduce errors, including security, performance, and semantic correctness.
Elements.Notes: A useful addition to standard code review checklists for AI-generated output is a prompt reproducibility check: can the reviewer understand what prompt produced this output, and does the output fully satisfy the design intent? This encourages transparency about AI use and supports iterative improvement.

Items.Text: Review AI-generated code for security vulnerabilities such as unsanitized inputs or improper dependency usage.
Check semantic HTML correctness, ensuring elements are used according to their intended purpose.
Evaluate performance implications of AI-generated code, including unnecessary re-renders or large bundle contributions.
Require that AI-generated contributions be traceable to a documented prompt for accountability and reproducibility.

Elements.Title: Preserving the Designer's Voice and Intent
Elements.BodyText: A critical challenge in AI-assisted design is ensuring that the final product reflects deliberate design decisions rooted in user research rather than defaulting to the generic patterns that AI tools favor.
Elements.Notes: Encourage students to maintain a design rationale document that records why key design decisions were made. When AI suggestions diverge from the design intent, this document provides the grounding to reject or redirect the AI's output confidently rather than defaulting to convenience.

Items.Text: Maintain a living design rationale document that records the reasoning behind key design decisions.
Actively compare AI-generated suggestions against user research insights to test their appropriateness.
Reject or revise AI outputs that produce conventional solutions where the user research calls for differentiated approaches.
Regularly revisit original user personas and scenarios to keep AI-assisted development anchored to user needs.

Topics.Title: Ethical Considerations and Professional Responsibility
Topics.Summary: Examines the ethical dimensions of using AI coding assistants in HCI work, including attribution, bias, intellectual property, and the professional responsibilities of designers who use AI tools. Encourages critical and reflective practice.

Elements.Title: Attribution and Transparency in AI-Assisted Work
Elements.BodyText: Designers and developers using AI coding assistants have a professional responsibility to be transparent about the role AI played in their work, particularly in academic, professional, and client-facing contexts.
Elements.Notes: Different institutional and professional contexts have varying norms around AI disclosure. Students should be aware of their institution's academic integrity policies as well as emerging industry standards. The general principle is that AI assistance should be acknowledged in the same way that any significant tool or resource contribution would be.

Items.Text: Disclose AI tool usage in project documentation, design handoffs, and academic submissions as appropriate.
Attribute AI-assisted contributions clearly in version control commit messages and design notes.
Transparency about AI use supports team trust and enables accurate assessment of project contributions.
Develop personal norms for AI disclosure that align with both institutional policies and professional ethics.

Elements.Title: Bias and Representation in AI-Generated Interfaces
Elements.BodyText: AI coding assistants trained on historical code and design data may reproduce biases related to cultural representation, gender, disability, and other dimensions of diversity in the interfaces they help generate.
Elements.Notes: Examples of AI-generated bias in interfaces include default avatar silhouettes that imply a specific body type, color schemes that fail for users with color vision deficiencies, or interaction patterns optimized for mouse users that exclude keyboard or assistive technology users. Critical review through a DEI lens is an essential quality practice.

Items.Text: Critically evaluate AI-generated interface content and imagery for unintended cultural or demographic bias.
Test generated interfaces with diverse user groups to surface bias that may not be apparent to the design team.
Use inclusive design checklists alongside AI-generated outputs to identify representation gaps.
Recognize that AI tools reflect the biases of their training data and require active human correction.

Elements.Title: Intellectual Property and Licensing Concerns
Elements.BodyText: AI coding assistants generate outputs derived from training data that may include proprietary or copyrighted code, raising unresolved questions about the intellectual property status of AI-generated artifacts.
Elements.Notes: This is an active area of legal debate. Students and practitioners should review the terms of service of the AI tools they use, be cautious about using AI-generated code in commercial products without legal review, and prefer tools that provide clear provenance and licensing information for their suggestions.

Items.Text: Review the terms of service of each AI tool to understand the ownership and licensing implications of generated outputs.
Be cautious about incorporating AI-generated code into commercial or client work without appropriate legal review.
Some AI tools provide provenance information indicating when suggestions are closely derived from specific training sources.
Establish team or organizational policies for acceptable use of AI-generated code in different project types.

Elements.Title: Maintaining Professional Competence
Elements.BodyText: Reliance on AI coding assistants without developing foundational design and development skills can create brittle competency, where practitioners are unable to critically evaluate, debug, or extend AI-generated outputs.
Elements.Notes: The analogy of a calculator and arithmetic is relevant here: calculators are powerful tools, but users who lack foundational numeracy cannot detect calculator errors. Similarly, designers who lack foundational HCI and coding knowledge cannot reliably evaluate AI-generated outputs for correctness or quality.

Items.Text: Develop and maintain foundational HCI and coding skills independent of AI tool assistance.
Use AI tools to extend and accelerate competence rather than to substitute for developing it.
Regularly practice tasks without AI assistance to maintain the ability to evaluate AI outputs critically.
Seek feedback from experienced practitioners on AI-assisted work to identify skill gaps that AI may be masking.

Elements.Title: Responsible AI Use in User-Facing Products
Elements.BodyText: When AI-assisted design and development produces interfaces that will be used by real people, designers bear responsibility for ensuring those interfaces are safe, trustworthy, and respectful of user autonomy.
Elements.Notes: This includes being thoughtful about AI-generated microcopy, persuasive patterns, and data collection interfaces that may have been generated efficiently but could manipulate or mislead users. The efficiency of AI-assisted production does not reduce the ethical weight of design decisions.

Items.Text: Apply the same ethical scrutiny to AI-generated interface copy and interaction patterns as to human-authored work.
Avoid using AI to scale production of dark patterns, manipulative design, or deceptive interfaces.
Ensure that AI-generated data collection interfaces accurately represent what data is collected and how it is used.
Center user wellbeing and autonomy as the primary design criteria when evaluating AI-generated outputs.
